Flow Lenia / synthetic morphospace

How much of a body survives its description?

Flow Lenia lets us see a body, the rule that produced it, and how both change under intervention. We put 25,167 synthetic specimens in the same twelve-dimensional shape map as 859 EmbryoMaker snapshots and 232 fish outlines. We then asked whether the same geometric structures appear across all three systems, and whether a path that returns to the same measured shape also returns to the same generating rule.

A closed path in shape space can leave the rule changed

The same twelve measurements find persistent loops in Flow Lenia, EmbryoMaker, and fish outlines. Inside Lenia, one 256-specimen neighborhood is unusually close to fish and shows a larger rule-state mismatch than the wider corpus after movement around closed paths in the map. The strict result remains narrow: the joint permutation is about p = 0.094, and none of the five fish-near candidates passed both dense controls.

Three systems, measured the same way

Every specimen is described by the same twelve normalized measurements. This lets us compare the datasets directly, while also setting a clear limit on what the map can know: two states can occupy the same coordinates when they differ in a rule variable that the measurements omit.

25,167 Flow Lenia specimens across several rule families
8,192 Single-family Lenia controls for exact loop calculations
859 EmbryoMaker morphology snapshots
232 Dryad fish body outlines
01 / From rules to measured forms

Each point still has a rule behind it

Each Flow Lenia specimen begins with a particular rule set. We run it, measure the body that forms, and place that body in the twelve-dimensional map. Different rules can land close together because the measurements record shape and motion rather than every internal parameter. Keeping the rule attached to each point lets us distinguish bodies that merely look alike from bodies produced in the same way.

Fish and embryo datasets give us shapes without their generating rules. Lenia gives us both. It therefore shows where a morphology map merges bodies that resemble one another but were produced differently.

02 / Persistent loops

Loop structure appears in all three datasets

A loop is a region of occupied shapes surrounding a region the system does not visit. The longest loop in the broad Lenia sample remains open as we widen each point's neighborhood by 2.78 normalized units. In exact dense runs, the single-family Lenia control reaches 0.80, fish reaches 0.64, and EmbryoMaker reaches 0.29. Interval counts cannot be compared across samples of different sizes, but the same calculation finds nontrivial holes in all three collections of shapes.

A loop gives us a return path around a gap. We can follow it back to the same measured neighborhood without retracing our steps, then check whether the rule state returned too.

03 / A fish-near neighborhood

One Lenia neighborhood is unusually close to fish

We chose a patch of 256 Lenia specimens from the synthetic cloud's own loop geometry before comparing it with either external dataset. Within this patch, the median distance to fish is 3.30 instead of 5.90 for the broad Lenia sample, while the median distance to EmbryoMaker rises from 4.46 to 11.98. Every specimen in the patch flips the combined fish-versus-EmbryoMaker score, and random patches do this about once in a thousand permutations.

The patch was selected from Lenia's geometry rather than its resemblance to fish. Its elongated, directional bodies entered the comparison afterward, so the agreement between geometry and appearance comes from two independent measurements.

04 / Closing the loop

The shape returns more often than the rule

We found 4,802 transport groups where a trajectory could be followed around a closed path in the measured map. Of these, 109 show more rule-state mismatch than their matched controls at all three scales under both closure measures. The combined count is only marginal under permutation, at about p = 0.094, although each measure separately has a stronger tail: about p = 0.008 for state and p = 0.0002 for ratio. Dense reruns leave one joint survivor among the five broad-corpus candidates and none among the five candidates from the fish-near patch.

The result is a tail, not a general rule

Some closed paths return to the same measured shape while leaving a difference in rule state, and the fish-near neighborhood shows more of this mismatch at the group level. We do not yet have a dependable per-specimen witness inside the patch because none of its five dense candidates passed both controls.

The twelve measurements can place two states together even when their rules differ. If that hidden difference later predicts a response to an obstacle, then it matters outside the measurement procedure because it changes what the body can do.

Transport finds rule differences inside the same measured shape

The same measurements recover structure shared across all three datasets. They also reveal where distinct rule states collapse onto one measured form. The map is useful for finding broad geometric organization, but it may be too coarse to predict how a particular specimen will respond.

The fish-near patch is where this distinction can be tested. It combines a lower distance to fish with an enriched difference in rule state, although neither measure was used to select the other. Dense validation keeps the claim precise: the enrichment belongs to the neighborhood, while a reliable per-specimen witness still has to be found.

If the obstacle test succeeds, one point on the map can contain several future responses. The current shape locates the body. Its rule state would help predict what the body does next.

Next experiment

Make the map predict an unseen response

Place an occluded obstacle in front of specimens from the existing compendium and record whether they turn away or die on contact. Then test, without changing the twelve measurements, whether the swervers occupy a connected region of the current map. If visually similar neighbors split by outcome, we can ask whether their remaining rule-state difference explains it.
